sections.h2: Who collects property tax in Wyoming, Michigan?
sections.html:
The City Treasurer's Office at City Hall, 1155 28th Street SW, Wyoming, MI 49509, collects city, county and school tax on real estate and personal property, along with utility bills and other city charges. Wyoming lies in Kent County, and the Kent County Treasurer picks up real property tax that is still unpaid on March 1.

The Assessor's Office sets values at the same building and keeps records for about 25,000 real and personal property parcels, including owner names, mailing addresses, structure photos, sketches, building permit lists and ownership transfer histories. The assessor line shown on the city's Board of Review page is 616-530-7231.

The Treasurer's drive-up window is behind City Hall and is staffed Monday through Thursday from 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

sections.h2: When are Wyoming property taxes due, and what are the late charges?
sections.html:
Summer tax is due August 31 and winter tax is due February 14. The city prints its penalties on the Treasurer page.

Wyoming tax due dates and late charges as printed on the city Treasurer page
BillDueLate charge
SummerAugust 314% interest added September 1, then 0.5% on the first of each month, to a maximum of 6%
WinterFebruary 143% interest penalty added February 15

Real property tax still due on March 1 goes to the Kent County Treasurer as delinquent. Personal property tax stays with the city and picks up 1% interest on the first of each month until paid.

Anyone closing between the two bills should know that a summer bill unpaid after August 31 starts costing money the next day. Ask the title company to confirm that the right bill is paid at closing.

sections.h2: How can I pay a Wyoming tax bill?
sections.html:
Payment is open at the counter, by mail, in the drop box or online. Cash or check at the Treasurer's Office carries no convenience fee.

  • Online payment runs through Invoice Cloud at wyomingmi.gov/payment, with a 2.7% fee on cards (minimum $1.95) and $0.80 on an e-check.
  • Cards are capped at $25,000 per payment and e-checks at $125,000.
  • The city's online options include Discover, MasterCard, American Express and Visa cards, PayPal, Venmo and e-checks.
  • Mail a check payable to the City of Wyoming with your payment stub or account number, or use the drop box at the northeast entrance to City Hall.
  • Payments received after 5:00 PM are credited the next day, and cash should never go by mail or in the drop box.

For a current balance on a parcel before closing, call the Treasurer's Office or use the property information link on its page.

sections.h2: How does Wyoming assess a home?
sections.html:
Michigan law has the city assess real property uniformly at 50% of the usual selling price. Wyoming says it appraises with a computer assisted mass appraisal system supplemented with current market data, and it multiplies true cash value by 50% to reach the assessed value.

The calendar is public. Notices of new assessed and taxable values are mailed on the last Friday in January. The assessor reviews taxpayer complaints from the first Monday in February through the second Thursday, and the roll is certified on the first Monday in March. For 2026 the assessor's review closed on February 12, and the March Board of Review closed on March 12.

Wyoming also posts a list of every parcel by address with the current value and most recent sale price, split into five alphabetical street ranges. That makes it simple to compare your home with neighbors before you file.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Wyoming assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the assessor's review in early February, then go to the March Board of Review if the answer does not settle it. The board meets in executive session on the Tuesday after the first Monday in March, begins hearing appeals on the second Monday, and finishes by the first Monday in April.

  • The Board of Review can raise, lower or sustain a value, add omitted property, and exempt poverty applicants and principal residences that were not on the prior roll.
  • July and December meetings are limited to clerical errors and mutual mistakes of fact. The assessor says they also take qualified agricultural exemptions, taxable uncappings and poverty exemptions.
  • The Michigan Tax Tribunal takes appeals after that. The assessor page says they must reach the State by May 31 for commercial and industrial property and by July 31 for residential property.

Members are appointed by City Council to three year terms. Each set of members includes a licensed real estate practitioner, a public accountant and a property owner of at least a year in the city.

sections.h2: Which exemptions matter when a Wyoming house changes hands?
sections.html:
The principal residence exemption removes up to 18 mills of school operating tax. To get it, you must own and occupy the home before June 1 for the summer bill or before November 1 for the winter bill. Owning or taking possession after November 1 qualifies you for the next tax year. The city notes that a form may have been signed at your closing, and says to submit one to the Assessor's Office if you are unsure.

Michigan allows only one such exemption. A rescind form has to be filed for your old homestead before you qualify for a new one, so a seller should confirm that the form was sent. Disabled veterans may qualify for a separate exemption with Form 5107 and Veterans Affairs documentation, and the city also asks for a driver's license copy.

The buyer owes a property transfer affidavit within 45 days. Wyoming warns that skipping it can mean additional tax owed back to the transfer date, plus penalties and interest. Taxable value is capped for the owner of record and resets to assessed value the year after a sale, so the first bill under a new owner is often higher.

sections.h2: What is Wyoming like for a seller?
sections.html:
Wyoming is the second most populous city in West Michigan, after Grand Rapids, which borders it on the northeast. It started as a farm township organized in 1848 and became a city in 1959 after disputes with Grand Rapids and Grandville over annexation. The 28th Street corridor, with Rogers Plaza and Studio 28, made it a regional retail center. Growth later moved southwest toward RiverTown Crossings, and the General Motors stamping plant closed in 2009. The 74 acre former GM property, called Site 36, is a redevelopment focus.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 78,588 residents, up from 76,501 in the 2020 census, spread over 24.74 square miles of land. In 2020 to 2024 data, 67.1% of housing is owner-occupied, the median value of an owner-occupied home is $225,200 and median gross rent is $1,196. There are 29,417 households averaging 2.61 people, the median household income is $73,677, and mean travel time to work is 21.9 minutes.

faqs.q: What are the Wyoming, Michigan property tax due dates?
faqs.a: Summer tax is due August 31 and winter tax is due February 14. Interest of 4% is added on September 1 for summer, with 0.5% monthly after that up to 6%. Winter takes a 3% penalty on February 15.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Wyoming property tax in person?
faqs.a: Pay at the Treasurer's Office in City Hall, 1155 28th Street SW, or at the drive-up window behind the building, which is staffed Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Cash and checks carry no convenience fee.

faqs.q: What happens to Wyoming tax unpaid on March 1?
faqs.a: Unpaid real property tax is turned over as delinquent to the Kent County Treasurer for continued collection. Personal property tax stays with the city and accrues 1% interest on the first of each month.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Wyoming property value?
faqs.a: Ask the assessor to review it in early February, then appeal to the March Board of Review, which begins hearings the second Monday in March. After that, residential owners can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31.

faqs.q: Do I lose my Wyoming homestead exemption when I sell?
faqs.a: The exemption ends with the sale, and a request to rescind should be filed for the old home. The buyer then claims it by owning and occupying the home before June 1 for the summer bill or November 1 for the winter bill.
